title: Breaking Down The Averbakh Variation | King's Indian | The Sensei Speedrun | GM Naroditsky

moves.spoken: d4, the knight to f6. We've been alternating between e4 and d4 — a chance to learn new positions, which can be exciting.
c4 — main-line d4 and c4.
g6 — a Grünfeld or a King's Indian.
The knight to c3, sticking to the main line.
Most people at this level don't play the Grünfeld — and indeed.
Black plays the King's Indian; our move is e4, the main line.
d6 — we reach the first tabia, a big branching point almost every King's Indian passes through, with ten or fifteen viable lines from here.
The line I recommend — underrated, poorly studied, one most King's Indian players pass by — is the Averbakh, named after Yuri Averbakh, and it starts with the bishop to e2.
Those versed in theory know the classical main line is the knight to f3 and the bishop to e2 —
— but in the Averbakh you develop the bishop to e2 and go straight for the bishop to g5 before the knight to f3.
Black castles.
The bishop to g5 — not just development, but a prophylactic move.
What does the bishop to g5 discourage? e5.
The first trap: e5 doesn't lose the game, but it loses a pawn and leads to a terrible endgame, which I'll show after. After h6 we have two moves — the bishop to h4, though h6 isn't that common —
— because it creates a target we can attack; the main move is to drop the bishop back to e3.

The bishop to e3 — preserving pressure on the h6-pawn, with the queen to d2 to follow, and h6 as a hook for a pawn storm. It's not automatic to castle kingside in the King's Indian; keeping the king in the centre, which is so well protected, lets you storm with g4, h4 and g5 straight at Black's king.
The downside of the bishop to e3 is that e5 becomes possible — but it's not the end of the world, just a typical King's Indian move. Why the bishop to e3 for the semi-Averbakh —

— because inducing h6 helps White; that pawn on h6 rather than h7 typically favors us. Now we close the centre with d5 — the whole point: closing it unties our hands for kingside action, since we no longer divert resources to hold the centre.

a5 — a typical King's Indian move preventing b4, usually followed by the knight maneuver to c5 via d7 or a6, pressuring e4. Another branching point; in the spirit of the Averbakh we go straight for Black's throat with a move that looks like a coffee-house move but is often the engine's top choice —
— not h4, though that's possible, but directly g4.
f4 is bad — it lets Black open the centre and activate the bishops; you almost never play f4 as White in these positions.

Full send g4. The idea is obvious: send the pawns at Black's king and open the h-file, using the h6-pawn as a hook — a pawn advanced past its start that acts like dynamite to blow open a file. Two things to mind: keep the e4-pawn protected — if Black's knight lands on c5 we play f3 to solidify e4, our main anchor; if the centre opens, the whole strategy collapses, so g4 and h4 depend entirely on keeping the centre closed. That's why, as Black, a common idea is to push c6, chipping at White's centre and preparing the queen to b6. Black can't fall asleep — the attack comes fast. Should we take the knight on c5? Almost never in the King's Indian: giving up the dark-squared bishop is a bad idea in maybe eighty percent of cases, because it lords over the position — controlling queenside squares, stopping the queen to b6 after c6, and above all supervising the pawn storm, controlling g5 and h6 and making h4 and g5 far stronger. It's a Swiss army knife; giving it up wrecks the dark squares, and after the d-pawn recaptures on c5 it hands Black the d6-square for the other knight.
The knight to a6. Do we need to stop the knight from reaching c5? No — as I just explained, it's fine —
— because we protect e4 with f3. So we continue the kingside campaign with h4, launching the second pawn. Why not g5 immediately? That was also very good, I agree —

— but the added benefit of h4 is that after g5 and the h-pawn takes g5, we recapture with the h-pawn and open the h-file. The knight to d7. Now a pleasant choice: h5, and Black closes with g5, which actually helps us — f5 becomes a gaping weakness and a coveted outpost for our knight. Or the queen to d2, but after the king to h7 it's hard to open the kingside; the knight to d7 was smart, so it's the classic situation where if we play g5 Black plays h5, and if we play h5 Black plays g5.
So we switch from tactics to positional play and play h5, inducing g5, then aim to bring the g1-knight around to f5 —
— which sounds very hard, but there's a typical maneuver in these positions.
The knight to f3, exploiting the temporary fact that the knight on d7 blocks the bishop —
— otherwise we couldn't play the knight to f3; and we deliberately don't put a pawn on f3, which would make navigating the knight over to f5 much harder.

The plan: get the knight to g3; Black will move the knight off d7 so the bishop controls f5, and we wait for the moment to plant the knight on f5. Meanwhile we shift the centre of our attention from the kingside to the queenside — a big misconception is that White can never attack the queenside in the King's Indian.
The knight to f6 — as predicted, Black moves off d7. In fact White has superiority on both flanks.
The knight to d2 — serving both purposes; then the knight to f1 and g3. Note the g4-pawn is very well protected.

The knight to c5, and now that our knight is off g1 we can play f3 very safely — not interfering with the knight's path from f1 to g3. Note the queen to c2 would have been a blunder, taking our eye off the g4-pawn; there's a strict order of operations. And we're not worried about king safety as long as the centre stays closed.
c6 — Black does everything right, but weakening f5 means Black is worse for the rest of the game. Do we take on c6 or on c5? No and no —
— White's job is to keep the centre closed. c6 and the trade on d5 don't open it much, so we continue routing the knight to g3.
Why don't we take the c5-knight? As I said, we don't give away the dark-squared bishop or create permanent dark-square weaknesses —
— this bishop is going to be a very important piece, trust me.
The pawn takes d5 — an interesting moment. We recapture with the c-pawn to keep the structure symmetrical; you consider the e-pawn recapture only when you control e4 —

— but the flaw here is that Black could advance e4, opening the centre and reopening the dark-squared bishop, the last thing we want. So the c-pawn takes. The c-file opens, but our queenside is perfectly defended; why not recapture with the knight —
— because the knight on c3 is important: it discourages b5, defends e4, protects d5 and guards b5. The bishop to d7.
The bishop to d7 doesn't threaten b5 yet — we have two defenders there. So finally, after about seven moves, we land the knight on g3. Long-term, our top goal is a specific minor-piece trade.

Not the dark-squared bishops — that Black bishop is terrible, a big pawn — the light-squared bishops: trade them and we land an uncontested knight on the f5-square, which just terrorizes Black. The queen to b6 hits b2; we must defend it.

Not b3 — that creates a queenside hook, allows a4 and loosens the knight on c3. We play the queen to d2 — harmonious, connecting the rooks and defending the bishop. Watch for the bishop takes g5, a frequently missed tactic: after the h-pawn takes g5, h6 can lead to a quick mate; Black defends with the knight to h7. Also, a nice square for the king is g2 — out of the way when the queenside opens.
On f2 the king is still susceptible to long-term tactics on g4 and c4. The rook to c8 — we can start walking the king toward g2.

The king to f2 — routed this way to keep the rooks connected, so we could bring a rook in urgently without the king to g2. We forfeit the bishop takes g5 for now. Why not castle? We can, but I want to keep the bishop takes g5 alive by leaving the rook on h1 — in closed positions you keep tactical possibilities open to keep the opponent on edge.
a4. Black wants a3, inducing b3, which loosens the knight on c3 with a rook on c8 and ideas like the queen to b4. There's a nice way to take the sting out of a3 —

— if Black plays a3 we meet it with b4, pinning the knight on c5; but playing a3 ourselves leaves a hole on b3, and after a3 Black has the knight to b3 hitting the queen. So the subtle rook to b1, planning to answer a3 with b4.

The rook to b1 protects b4. The queen to a5 — Black shows keen King's Indian knowledge, but now we're almost ready for the bishop takes g5. Let's calculate: the bishop takes g5, the h-pawn takes g5, h6, and after the bishop to h8 the problem is that if we take on g5 with check the king hides on h7; so we need to open the h-file for the other rook to jump to h1 — meaning after the bishop to h8 we play h7, forcing the knight to take on h7, and there's a critical move.

The bishop takes g5 — I briefly checked the knight takes e4 with check and made sure Black has no shenanigans with the knight takes c4; the counterplay comes too late, since the queen to a5 shows Black wants to push to b4, and there isn't time.
The h-pawn takes g5 — we're already checkmating the black king.
The h-pawn takes g5, and of course h6.
h6, the bishop to h8.
h7 with check. Why not the queen takes g5 —
— very tempting, since the king hides on h7. I actually spotted a cool idea, an almost-immortal concept, but it doesn't quite do the trick —
— and it isn't necessary; h7 is a much simpler way to win. Let's stick to our guns with h7.
The knight takes h7, and the rook takes h7 — without this move the whole combination would fall apart.
The king takes on h7. The necessary component of the entire combination was actually putting our king on f2. What's the best move now? Not the rook to h1 —

— because Black plays the king to g6 and defends g5. So instead the queen takes g5, cutting the king off the g-file, and next we swing the rook to h1 with mate. Black's only try is the bishop to g7 to block g8, but then the rook to h1 forces the king back to g8, and the winning move is the knight to h5.

There we threaten both the queen takes g7 and the knight to f6 mate. Interestingly, after h6 earlier Black had a ridiculous defensive resource that might have held on, still much worse — I'll show it in the post-game. We could also start with the knight to h5; either way it's all over. Great game — only twenty-seven moves, and yet a lot to talk about.
